asSun.p: The Hermit is Virgo's card, so with your Sun in Virgo this one's yours before anything else in the chart gets a say. Mercury rules Virgo. The Sun has no special dignity in this sign. It's a visitor there, and a visitor ends up doing things the way the house does them, so Mercury colours a lot of how you shine. In practice you work out who you are by thinking it through, sorting and checking, and a day where you finally understood something properly does a lot for your confidence. Have a look at the old man in the picture. He's on a peak in the snow with his lantern held out at shoulder height, and he's looking down at the ground just in front of him. It's a small light and it shows him the next few steps. Virgo is mutable earth, earth that can still be dug over and reshaped, and most Virgo Suns I've seen treat themselves that way, as something still being worked on, a bit at a time.

Most of it happens in your head, and quite a lot of it happens late at night. You replay the meeting and find the one sentence you'd change. You read the group chat, draft a reply, trim it, trim it again, and send something shorter than what you meant. A friend asks where you'd like to eat and you give them three options with reasons, when what you actually wanted was the Thai place. Your sense of yourself is tied up with being useful and getting things right, so a day where you fixed something, even a dripping tap or a messy spreadsheet, feels like a good day in a way that's hard to explain to a Leo. And you need time alone to know what you think. After a big family weekend you usually need a whole evening with the door shut before you feel like yourself again.

The obvious gift is your eye for detail, and everyone mentions it. The less obvious one is that you can hold a question open for a very long time without panicking. Other people need an answer by Friday. You can sit with not knowing for months, keep looking, and wait until the true thing shows itself, and most of your good decisions come out of that patience. I've seen a Virgo Sun spend a year quietly deciding whether to leave a job and a city, and then leave cleanly, no drama, no regret, because the thinking had actually been done. You're also hard to talk into things. A salesman, a charming new boss, a friend with a scheme, and you listen politely, go home, check the numbers, and ring back with two questions they can't answer.

The shadow isn't really the criticism, you know about that one. It's that you can make a private project out of not being ready. The course you'll enrol in once you've read up on it. The business you'll start after one more year of saving. The novel that's been in a drawer since you were twenty-six because the first chapter still isn't right. Mutable earth will happily rework a thing forever, and a Virgo Sun can use that as a reason never to call it ready. You call it being careful, and some of it is. A lot of it is fear of being seen doing something badly in public. Meanwhile someone with half your ability and none of your standards goes ahead and does it, and you read about them.

When something goes wrong, a Virgo Sun makes a list. A parent in hospital, a round of redundancies, a breakup, and within a day you've got the phone numbers, the forms, the rota for who visits when. It works, and people are grateful. Then about a week in, the Mercury side turns on you. You stop sleeping properly, you check the same email four times, and you start finding fault with small things at home because the big thing can't be fixed. Your partner loads the dishwasher wrong and gets the full weight of a month's worry. The people around you feel managed and a bit told off. What helps is getting out of your head through your body. A long walk with no podcast, a garden bed, cooking something slow. And one person who's allowed to say 'that's enough for today' and take the list off you.

Love, for a Virgo Sun, mostly looks like doing things. You notice your partner's car is due for a service and book it. You remember they can't stand coriander. Saying it is harder, which is fine until the day they need it said. The less obvious problem is that you can treat a partner the way you treat yourself, as a work in progress. The article about sleep you forwarded, the better way to word their email to the landlord, the gentle note about their posture. You mean it kindly, and after a year or two it can feel to them like being marked. Pisces is your opposite sign, and The Moon is its card, so the people who get under your skin are often vague and dreamy and hopeless with calendars. They're usually the ones you learn most from. Pick one thing about your partner you've been quietly correcting and leave it alone for a month.

Virgo's natural house is the sixth, the daily grind, the job as it's actually done on a wet Tuesday, so work feeds your sense of who you are more than it does for most signs. You need to be good at something specific. Being a generalist leaves you uneasy. You're the one who knows where the error in the spreadsheet is, who reads the contract all the way through, who fixes the process nobody else noticed was broken, and you're usually underpaid for it because it looks easy when you do it. The trap is staying years in a role you mastered long ago, because being the expert feels safe and being new at something feels like being bad at it. I've seen Virgo Suns turn down a promotion for exactly that reason. Ask for the title and the money that match what you actually do, and take the list of what that is into the meeting.

At twenty a Virgo Sun is often hard on itself in a way that looks like shyness from outside. You're watching everyone, you've worked out who's pretending, and you don't trust yourself to say so. You over-prepare for everything and under-apply for everything. Through the thirties the skill starts to pay, because by then you really do know your field better than most, and people start asking you. That's usually the decade you learn that your standards belong to you, and you can lower them in a few places without the sky falling in. The fifties tend to bring some ease about being good at things. The work doesn't have to prove anything any more, and a lot of Virgo Suns take up something they're hopeless at, the cello, Italian, a pottery class, for the fun of being a beginner. The ones who don't loosen up can get fussy and a bit lonely, correcting the waiter.

Pick one thing you've been getting ready to do for more than a year. Put it out into the world in a rough state, on purpose. Send the draft, book the first lesson, post the thing with the typo still in it. Set a timer for twenty minutes, do it, and stop when it rings, whether it's finished or not. Afterwards write down what actually happened. It's almost always smaller than what you'd been bracing for.

asMoon.p: Your Moon was in Virgo when you were born, and The Hermit is Virgo's card, so this is the card for how you feel things and what you need before you feel safe. The Moon has no special dignity in Virgo. It gets no help there and no trouble either, and Mercury, which rules the sign, gets into everything it does. That's why your feelings tend to arrive with a commentary attached. You feel something, you look at it, and then you ask whether it's reasonable to feel it at all. Virgo is earth, so the body's in on it as well, and since the Moon looks after the body's rhythms, a mood usually shows up in your stomach or your sleep before you've got words for it. Look at where the old man on the card has chosen to stand, right up high and on his own. Most Virgo Moons have a version of that spot, the car parked outside the house for ten minutes before going in, the walk before anyone else is up.

You tidy when you're anxious. You might not have noticed, but everyone you live with has. A row with your sister on the phone, and within ten minutes you're wiping down the bench or sorting the spice drawer, and it helps, even though the bench was already clean. You also need a routine, probably more than you'd admit. The same breakfast, the same walk, the same side of the bed. A holiday with no plan can leave you jumpy by day three. When a friend cancels at the last minute you say it's fine and it is, mostly, and you use the evening better than the dinner would have been. And you read people's small signals very closely. A shorter text than usual, a colleague who says good morning without looking up, and you'll turn it over all afternoon.

People feel looked after around you in small, exact ways. You notice that a friend has stopped eating properly before they've noticed themselves, and you turn up with soup, and you don't make a speech about it. The less obvious gift is how well you can be alone. Plenty of people are frightened of an empty weekend. You can go away for three days on your own with a book and come back steadier, and because you can settle yourself like that, you don't lean too hard on anyone. When someone near you is falling apart, you're also very good at the practical next step. Their dad's just died and they can't think, and you quietly find the funeral director's number and put the kettle on.

Because your feelings come with a critic built in, you can talk yourself out of needing anything. You're sad, a voice says it's silly to be sad about that, so you don't mention it, and nobody knows. A few months of that and the people close to you honestly think you're fine. The other thing is worry dressed up as care. You check the stove twice, you look up the rash online at midnight, you ask your partner whether they've taken their tablets, and it feels like love, and some of it is. A lot of it is you being frightened and dealing with it by checking. A Virgo Moon can also hold on to a small criticism for years. Your mum said something about your cooking in 2009 and you still season more carefully when she visits.

The first thing a Virgo Moon does under stress is withdraw and get busy. Grief, a breakup, bad news in the family, and you're cleaning the oven at eleven at night and answering every email within the hour. Nobody sees you cry. A week later it's gone into your body, usually the stomach, sometimes the skin or the sleep, and you've gone quiet in a way that's hard for the people around you to read. They ask what's wrong and you give them a precise, reasonable answer that has nothing to do with it. Your household ends up tiptoeing, because you're being very nice and very tense at the same time. What helps is someone who'll sit with you without asking you to explain it. Plain food, early nights, a walk somewhere green, and a bit of permission to be useless for a day.

You need someone who notices the small stuff, because the small stuff is how you say it. If you've learnt how they take their coffee and after a year they still haven't learnt yours, it hurts more than you'll ever say out loud. You feel safe with people who are reliable in boring ways. They text when they said they would. They don't make plans and forget them. The less obvious thing is how badly you take being looked after. You're sick in bed, your partner brings you soup, and within ten minutes you're up rinsing the pot and telling them you're fine. Letting someone care for you clumsily, the wrong soup, the pillow in the wrong place, is something most Virgo Moons have to practise. Next time you're unwell, stay in bed and let them get it wrong.

Your mood at work depends heavily on whether the place is in order. A messy handover, a manager who changes the plan every Monday, a desk next to the printer in an open-plan office, and you're drained by lunch even when the work itself is easy. You do well with a routine you can trust and a task you can finish. Ticking something off matters to you emotionally, which is why endless projects with no clear end can slowly flatten you. You're often the colleague others come to when they're overwhelmed, and you'll sit with them and break the thing into pieces. That's kind, and it's also how you end up carrying everyone's worry home in the car. Keep one part of the day that nobody else gets, even fifteen minutes with the door closed or a walk at lunch.

In your twenties a Virgo Moon is often anxious in a way other people don't see. You're keeping everything in order and privately sure you're getting it wrong, and you might lean on routines, diets, cleaning or study a bit harder than you need to. By the mid-thirties you've usually learnt what actually settles you, and it tends to be simpler than you expected. Enough sleep, a clear kitchen, time alone, a person who's easy to be around. The self-criticism is still there, but you've started answering it back. The fifties tend to bring a kinder relationship with your own body and your own mistakes. Plenty of Virgo Moons find that's when they stop apologising for wanting a quiet night in, and just have one, without a reason ready.

When you catch yourself tidying, checking or re-reading because you feel uneasy, stop for one minute. Put the cloth or the phone down. Ask yourself, in so many words, 'what am I actually feeling?' and wait for a one-word answer, like tired or lonely or scared. Say the word out loud, even if nobody's in the room. Then go back to the tidying if you still want to. Most of the time you won't need to.

asRising.p: Virgo was coming over the eastern horizon at the moment you were born, and whichever sign does that becomes your first house, the one about your body, your manner, and how you walk into things. With Virgo rising, Mercury rules your whole chart. That's a big deal. The planet of noticing and talking and working things out is the one steering, so wherever Mercury sits in your chart matters more for you than it would for most people. The Hermit is Virgo's card, which puts him at your front door. Look at him with his hood up, lantern out, staff in the other hand, waiting quietly. Strangers get that first. Someone composed, a little held back, clearly paying attention. Mutable earth at the front of the chart means you're adaptable in company and you do fit the room after a while, though the first ten minutes are always a bit careful.

You check a room before you walk into it. At a party you find the kitchen, or the one person you know, or a useful job like opening the wine, and you watch for a while before you join anything. In a job interview you're neat, prepared, slightly formal, and you've probably read the company's annual report. People ask you for directions in the street, and it's because you look like someone who'd know. You tend to start things by researching them, so the first week of any new hobby is mostly reading. And there's usually something tidy about how you present, even when you're relaxed. The good shoes, the clean nails, the bag with everything in its own pocket. Your friends tease you about it, and you don't mind, much.

People trust you quickly, and it's because you look like you'd tell them the truth. That's rare. Strangers at work bring you the problem they're embarrassed about, the form they don't understand, the mistake they haven't admitted to their boss yet, and you deal with it without any fuss or judgement. The less obvious gift is that your reserve protects you. You don't give much away early, so you get a good long look at people before they get a look at you, and your first read on someone is usually right. I've seen a Virgo rising sit through a whole dinner with a sister's new boyfriend, say almost nothing, and then name exactly what was off about him on the drive home. A year later everyone agreed.

The careful manner can harden into a closed one. You come across as cool, or judging, when really you're shy and working out where to stand. New colleagues decide you don't like them. A partner's friends think you're stuck up after the first barbecue, because you spent it helping in the kitchen and hardly spoke. And because Mercury runs the chart, the running commentary is always on, and sometimes it leaks out through your face. Someone tells a story badly and you wince. A friend shows you the flat they've just bought and your eyes go straight to the damp patch, and they see it. Virgo rising also tends to cover its own body's signals with a busy, capable surface, so you can look perfectly fine while running on four hours' sleep and cold coffee.

When things go wrong you get calmer on the outside, which confuses people. The car's been stolen, the project's collapsed, someone's said something cruel, and your face goes neutral and your voice gets very even, and people assume you're fine. Your first instinct is to fix the practical bit, so you're on the phone to the insurance company within the hour. About a week later the stress comes out through the body, the gut or the back or a twitching eye, and you're irritable in a small, precise way that's hard to argue with. The people closest to you get the sharp comments strangers never see, and they start to feel they're the problem. What helps is someone who knows you well enough to look past the calm and say so, and a morning off where nobody needs an answer from you.

With Virgo rising, Pisces falls on your seventh house, the house of partners, so the people you end up with are often softer and more dreamy than the face you show the world. They're artistic, or spiritual, or a bit disorganised, and they see straight through the tidy surface to the person underneath, which is unnerving and also what you wanted. You tend to be slow to start. You'd like to know someone for a while before anything happens, and early dates can feel like interviews to the other person. Sagittarius sits on your fourth house, home, so behind closed doors you're looser and funnier, and more restless, which people at work would never guess. Let a partner see that side early, the silly voices, the sudden plan to drive somewhere for the weekend.

Gemini lands on your tenth house, career, and Mercury rules both Gemini and your chart, so work and the way you present yourself are tied together tightly. You often end up in jobs that use language or information. Editing, teaching, analysis, the admin that keeps a whole office running, anything where you're the go-between. You interview well because you prepare, and you keep jobs because you're reliable in a way managers notice after about three months. The risk is that you look so competent at the start that people hand you everything, and you don't know how to say no without it sounding like failure. Gemini on the tenth also means you like variety in your working life, even if your manner suggests otherwise. Two roles, a side project, a change every few years, that usually suits you better.

At twenty Virgo rising often looks older than it is. You're the sensible friend, the one who remembers the tickets and knows when the last train goes. Some of that is real and some of it is you not yet knowing how else to be. By the mid-thirties the manner has usually loosened. You've found the people who get past the careful bit quickly, and you're less worried about being read as cold. The Gemini tenth house often brings a career change or two in this stretch. The fifties tend to be kind to Virgo rising. The neatness turns into a quiet sort of authority, and people start deferring to you on things you've been right about for decades. The body usually needs steadier upkeep by then, and you're better at giving it that than most.

At the next gathering where you only know a few people, give yourself one small rule. Within the first ten minutes, before you've found a job to do, walk up to one stranger and ask them a real question about themselves. Let your face do what it wants while they answer. No wine to pour, no dishes, nothing in your hands. Notice how long it takes them to relax with you. It's usually quicker than you'd think.

asBirthCard.p: This card comes from your birthdate and nothing else in the chart. Add up every digit of the date. If the total's over 22, add its digits together and keep going until it isn't. Yours comes to nine, which is The Hermit. Nine is the last of the single numbers, so it's where a count finishes before it starts again at ten, and it's three threes, the same small thing grown three times over. In the Majors it comes straight after Strength, where you learn to handle something wild, and just before the Wheel of Fortune, where life starts turning around you again. The Hermit sits between the two, off on his own, working out what he's learnt. The card's own sign is Virgo, careful and earthy and ruled by Mercury, and that flavour comes with the card whatever signs are in your own chart.

It tends to show up as needing to understand a thing before you'll take part in it. At school you were the one who kept asking why, and it wasn't to be difficult. You honestly couldn't learn something without knowing what it was for. At work you go quiet in the planning meeting and then send a long, careful email that evening that changes the plan. You probably have a subject, or a few, that you know an unusual amount about, and it grew out of long stretches of reading or tinkering on your own. There's often a pattern of pulling back every few years too. After a breakup, a move or a bad job, you drop off the social calendar for a season and come back different, a bit clearer. Your friends have learnt not to worry when it happens.

The gift is that the time alone keeps paying out. Each withdrawal leaves you with something solid, a skill, a clearer idea of what you want, a decision you won't have to make twice. People with this birth card often end up being the one others ask, because over the years you've thought through things most people only react to. A friend's marriage is wobbling, a cousin's thinking of dropping out of uni, and they ring you, because they know you'll ask a better question than anyone else. The less obvious part is that you're good at letting people find their own answer. You say what you've noticed and then step back, and they leave feeling it was their idea, which it partly was.

The retreat that helps can also become the place you live. A hard year, and you pull back, which is fine, but then pulling back becomes the habit and five years pass with the same three people and the same routines. You tell yourself you're just private. Some of it is that you've got used to never being disappointed by anyone, because you never quite let anyone near enough to do it. The other shadow is a kind of quiet superiority. Because you've thought hard about things, you can get impatient with people who haven't. At a dinner you'll sit through someone's confident, wrong opinion about house prices with a small, closed smile, and everyone at the table can see it.

Under pressure, a Hermit birth card goes to ground. Someone dies, the job goes, a relationship ends, and your first move is to cancel everything and stay in. You want silence and you want to think, and for a few days that's exactly right. A week later, though, you might still be in there, reading everything about the problem and talking to nobody about it, and the people who love you are texting and getting one-line replies. They feel shut out, and they're worried in a way you don't see, because from inside, the quiet feels productive. What helps is keeping one thread open on purpose. One friend, one walk a day with someone, one meal a week at someone else's table. Take the solitude, and let somebody know where you've gone.

You love slowly and privately, and the people who get close to you have usually waited a while. That's fine, and the ones worth having don't mind. The harder bit is that you tend to fall for the idea of someone first, turn them over in your head for weeks, and then find the real person a bit noisier than the version you'd been thinking about. Give the real one a chance. You also need a partner who can be in the house with you without needing conversation, and who takes long silences as company. When you do open up, it's all at once, usually late at night, and you say more in an hour than you've said in a month. Tell your partner that's how you work, so they know to wait for it.

Nine as a working pattern suits depth. You tend to do best in work you can go into and stay in for years. Research, a trade, a specialism, counselling, writing, the one corner of the law nobody else wants to learn. An open-plan office with a chat window going all day usually wears you out. The pattern also has a teaching turn to it. Around the middle of a career, people with this card often start training others, and they're good at it, because they remember exactly how hard it was to learn. What costs you at work is going quiet at the wrong moment. You've thought it through, you know the answer, and you let the loud person in the meeting win because speaking up felt like too much. Say it anyway, even if it comes out a bit clumsy.

In your twenties the Hermit pattern can feel like being out of step. Everyone else is going out and you're reading, or you're going out and wishing you were reading. You may go through a few long stretches alone that look to other people like being lost. Through the thirties it starts to make sense. The things you worked out on your own turn into real knowledge, and you find a few people who don't mind your quiet. This is often when a vocation settles. By the fifties, people with this birth card tend to have become the one others seek out, the teacher, the elder in a family, the person at work who knows why things are done the way they are. The risk then is getting a bit fixed and cut off. The ones who do it well keep a couple of young people in their lives.

Once a month, take half a day entirely on your own with no screens. A walk, a notebook, a café in a suburb where nobody knows you. Before you go, write one question you're chewing on at the top of a page. At the end, write whatever answer you've got, even a half one. Then, within the next two days, tell one person what you worked out. The telling is the part people with this card tend to skip.
